I doubt I'm alone in being someone who remembers the story arc of these games rather than particular puzzles after any time passes. In that category the game provides a satisfying ending to the ongoing conflict and is the most "cinematic" of the installments that came before it.  The script and voice acting seemed better assembled as well.

Enigmatis 3 felt shorter, but that could be because of a less convoluted progression with more tightly designed puzzle destination than less meaningful content. If you play the Engimatis series one after the other this third act will feel like the "thrilling conclusion" but might feel previous installments had more engaging and satisfying (and alternatively frustrating )  puzzles. Enigmatis 2 may be the strongest in all categories, but the series taken as a whole stands out in a genre that could be much stronger overall.

Enigmatis 3 shows mastery when it comes to polish, pacing, visuals and fully customisable difficulty options. The puzzles remain logical enough without being too easy. There is so much variety with the mini-games, exploration and detective part, that you almost forget it’s a hidden object game at heart. The story is clearly explained and it’s concluded satisfyingly. I say this as a fan who replayed the previous Enigmatis games just before playing this one.

That said, do keep in mind how the game is smaller and more linear compared to the previous games. While there is still fast travel, lots of areas become inaccessible and there is less need to fast travel anyway. I’m not saying this as a bad thing perse, but I’m sure there are some longtime fans who might dislike the change. What I am more annoyed about is how some achievements are permanently missable and it’s made worse with the save system (the game saves constantly and there is no manual save). The only option you have is completing the game and then playing it for the second time to get whatever you missed. 

Artifex Mundi games have always been high quality, this one doesn’t disappoint. I can safely recommend it to fans of these games. New players are better off starting with the previous two as they’re a trilogy. The price of around €15 is fair enough considering the quality you’re getting. It took me 8 hours to complete the game and get all the achievements. First run was around 5.4 hours, the rest was the second run by skipping everything as much as possible just to get the remaining collectibles. The achievements are generally fine. Some are story related, a lot involve collectibles, not skipping mini-games and not using hints for the hidden object portion.

2016 was the year of Endless Fables: The Minotaur's Curse and Enigmatis 3: The Shadow of Karkhala. They have two similarities moreover: both are impeccable games released the same year.

The Shadow of Karkhala brought in an absolutely phenomenal introduction to the game, the finest of them all across the trilogy. Animations and cutscenes were spectacular in quality, proving that 2016 was definitely a great era for Artifex Mundi. If we speak about novelty, the loading screen when you enter the game, save, and quit is really unique. I have not seen such in other 2016 AM games. The story has a fascinating twist as you progress towards this end, but I was still absolutely speechless from the get-go. I had a hunch the twist was going to happen, but it still caught me off-guard.

While I rain praises for this game's delivery, I had caught eye with some inconsistencies as well. Puzzles are very basic, very common, and very AM. Nothing is much new about it and I have no other comments about it. The voice acting was delivered not too great, but the whole story and quality of the visuals make up for it. There was also no indicators for collectibles and some are very hard to see. If you're a casual not looking to complete all the achievements, you don't have to worry.

Speaking of a complete achievements run, a 100% one-run is possible for Steam's achievements, but do note that there is a few achievements ingame that Steam does not count. This is particular to the alternate gamemode when playing the HO scenes. If you want to finish the achievements ingame, you may have to do a second run of the main story. If you wish to do a  100% achievements run based on Steam's, then one run will suffice. 

This was such a wonderful treat to end the trilogy, and a big respect to this release. Truly spectacular. I am more than impressed ever since I started the game, and even more so when I finished it. It took me about 3 hours for overall gameplay, including the side story. 

As I wrap up this long review for this game, I will be placing this game a [u]9/10[/u] rating. All factors attributed to my experience and points I mentioned a few paragraphs back. This game is a sure recommend, but even so, play the entire trilogy first before you play this!

The final entry in the series is certainly much prettier than [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198030806206/recommended/284750?snr=1_5_9__402]the first[/url] or [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198030806206/recommended/284770?snr=1_5_9__402]second[/url] games. The (non-HO) locations look much better, which is welcome since you will spend most of your time in these games doing anything and everything but actual HO puzzles.

One aspect of the genre's transition toward a more narrative, naturalistic adventure format is that the HO scenes, inasmuch as they still exist, have transformed into something much less fun. Let me explain: HO games of old, even though they had about 25% of the pixels to work with, made every object visually clear and identifiable. They largely relied on juxtaposition to make the scenes interesting. That is to say, they had a lot of objects in unexpected places, but once you found one it was obvious what it was, and surprising that you didn't see it earlier. This is the same principle used by magicians: people think they observe the world as it is, but actually most of our perception is just assumptions about the way things *should* be. When we notice this, it fills us with a kind of awe and whimsy, and that was part of the charm of old hidden object games and books. This gave them a surreal look, that would be (or was) often absurd in the context of a conventional narrative (which the very early games didn't have at all). 

But, in more recent games such as this, in the interest of making these scenes blend in with the rest of the game, which HO is now only a minor part of, the scenes are made to look more and more "plausible," and so the tricks they use have to change: I see a lot more ambiguous or partially obscured objects, and objects whose line and color are intentionally muddy. There are far fewer "how did I miss that?" moments and far more "what is that?" moments. Instead of a magic show it ends up feeling more like cleaning your room or organizing a deceased parent's estate.

For a further exposition on the issues I have with Artifex and the modern HOG swill mill, see my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198030806206/recommended/284850?snr=1_5_9__402]review of Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride[/url]. 

If I was reading a (graphic) novel, I would expect better writing. If I was playing an adventure game, I'd expect more interesting, challenging, and original puzzles (and better writing). If I was playing a hidden object game, I'd expect to spend most of my time on (better) hidden object puzzles. Because I'm playing a game from this Frankenstein HOPA genre, all these expectations are subverted, and I can somnambulate through the succession of short mediocre encounters before any of them annoys me enough to judge it very harshly,  but it is equally hard to say that it is actually any good.

The final chapter and conclusion to the Enigmatis storyline. 

As I mentioned on my 2nd review, just like movies, the storylines start dwindling as they make more of them without the same love or passion as they did the first. That happened here too.

The story felt quite a bit distant from the last game, let alone the one from the first. That gloomy mystery scenario was no longer there and instead it was switched with some very bright, white snowy mountains. The story still has the same end goal which is [spoiler] get to the priest and destroy his evilness [/spoiler] but it feels detached from the gloomy mysterious atmosphere prevalent in the previous two.

Voice over and animations were much better than the previous two, but the game also came out later, so it had the benefits of better technology. It had "mini games" or mini events from time to time [spoiler] like climbing up a mountain [/spoiler] that added a little something to the game play but besides that the puzzles and hidden object scenes were pretty good. Not too hard, not too easy. The point and click elements were also good trying to solve and find items to know where to go or what to do next.  [b] Easter egg [/b] Her car keys (I believe they were hers) had a key charm with the Artifex logo. 

The one thing that bummed me out about game play was that the objects that are picked up along the way are not [i] as [/i] reusable as they used to be. Very few objects were reusable compared to previous games. It's something small, but that I really enjoyed in previous games. 

All in all, I recommend the game and the whole series. It does have a full arc and a conclusion that doesn't leave you wanting. I'd say this is probably one of the best series in Artifex Mundi's library. Oh, and remember to play the bonus chapters!
